e-12562.problem:
Determine the quadratic Taylor polynomial for the function of two variables 
$f(x,y) = \cos(x+y)$
about the point $(0,0).$
e-12562.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y) = (0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\,+\,y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}((-1)\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12563.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form
e-12563.problem:
For the function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R,$ defined as

$$
f\left(x,y \right) 
=
x^2y-xy^3,
$$

determine the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/b799b1e1fbe7819de86c131989530033d750669ddc8fee88c711b537dad982a6.png) Give your answer in matrix form.
e-12563.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/b1c2d4408c64daf16466d81c1ea97bdd32f821deb858cd09bc539fc53ebf3ad8.png) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/c54318fa746f53209585695e2c40d80d793d2b35327b257426b4e4fa7b25463b.png)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/952dafd201f20f1da5b0ac77527beeb4f6d7c259813dbaee74a8d6796dd5d3b2.png)

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-{y}^{3} & {x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x-3{y}^{2} \\ 2x-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial (in matrix form) is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/fc105c91cf998f6b564570697321cfb72ac30f81e88dd6c1a0decfe8495259ba.png)

e-12564.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,0) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/32af7a7ab867c247eff15583688e31052e2d640b1be6c6c1b1f8bd19b7b7f2f7.png) to approximate the value of $f(1,1,1).$
e-12564.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/f27bcd29776525aa543b778627e0aace4e0b0537ceac83f5750a31f5def4f762.png) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/c281563d780c34ea5753498e0e722bfb0296fe06c5d43e82473a45901a1aa7ee.png)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/2fa9abbaad8230a38e1085b8842fbbd970c66addff6f388e13973ee116f0cd37.png)

In this case, we have ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/71175744ceb56efc01b8b18b97d6681b11b8e9b85a1d899fc9a137ab5e3c611c.png) and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/0d3a22cd82a02ab5122e811236d53eb4c0018e9817d2542163acc005ca5d3764.png)

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/dad24b303457c56dc14c11b3b9de6cb827b18b8f3a03059922d1b15521ea119d.png) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+1+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using e^u=1+u+O(u^2) with u=x^2+y^2, the quadratic Taylor polynomial is 1+x^2+y^2. Thus a=b=c=1 and a+b+c=3.

For the function of two variables f(x,y)=ex2+y2, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about (0,0) is given by f(x,y)=a+bx2+cy2. Find the value of a+b+c.

a
2
b
6
c
8

4
e
3

Correct
EXPLANATION

If the function f(x,y) is twice differentiable at (x,y)=(0,0), then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about (0,0) is given by f(x,y)≈f(0,0)+fx(0,0)⋅x+fy(0,0)⋅y⏞Linear approximation≈+12(fxx(0,0)⋅x2+2fxy(0,0)⋅xy+fyy(0,0)⋅y2)⏟Quadratic part.

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have f(0,0)=1.

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: fx(x,y)=2xex2+y2,fy(x,y)=2yex2+y2fx(0,0)=0,fy(0,0)=0

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: fxx(x,y)=2(1+2x2)ex2+y2,fxx(0,0)=2fxy(x,y)=4xyex2+y2,fxy(0,0)=0fyy(x,y)=2(1+2y2)ex2+y2,fyy(0,0)=2

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by f(x,y)≈1+0⋅x+0⋅y+12(2⋅x2+2(0)⋅xy+2⋅y2)=1+1x2+1y2.

Finally, a+b+c=1+1+1=3.

For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=2{e}^{x-y},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax-2y+b{x}^{2}+cxy+{y}^{2}.
$$

after.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =2, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+2\cdot x+(-2)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-2)\cdot xy+2\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+2x-2y+1{x}^{2}+(-2)xy+{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b=2+1+(-2)=1.
$$

f(x,y)=1+a{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.

after.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(2)\cdot xy+(-4)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{2}+2xy+(-2){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
a+b+c=(-\frac{1}{2})+2+(-2)=-\frac{1}{2}.

Question 3

For the function of two variables f(x,y)=cos⁡(x−2y), the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about (0,0) is given by f(x,y)=1+ax2+bxy+cy2. Find the value of a+b+c.

a
2
b
−12
c
3
d
32
e
−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If the function f(x,y) is twice differentiable at (x,y)=(0,0), then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about (0,0) is given by f(x,y)≈f(0,0)+fx(0,0)⋅x+fy(0,0)⋅y⏞Linear approximation≈+12(fxx(0,0)⋅x2+2fxy(0,0)⋅xy+fyy(0,0)⋅y2)⏟Quadratic part.

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have f(0,0)=1.

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: fx(x,y)=−sin⁡(x−2y),fy(x,y)=2sin⁡(x−2y)fx(0,0)=0,fy(0,0)=0

  • Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following: fxx(x,y)=−cos⁡(x−2y),fxx(0,0)=−1fxy(x,y)=2cos⁡(x−2y),fxy(0,0)=2fyy(x,y)=−4cos⁡(x−2y),fyy(0,0)=−4

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by f(x,y)≈1+0⋅x+0⋅y+12(−1⋅x2+2(2)⋅xy+(−4)⋅y2)=1+(−12)x2+2xy+(−2)y2.

Finally, a+b+c=(−12)+2+(−2)=−12.

content.problem:
For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y),$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=1+a{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
content.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(2)\cdot xy+(-4)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{2}+2xy+(-2){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=(-\frac{1}{2})+2+(-2)=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Question 6
?

For the function f:R2→R, defined as

f(x,y)=xsin⁡(x−y),

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[11] is given by

f(x)≈∗+[1∗][∗y−1]+12[∗y−1]T[∗−1−10][∗y−1].

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.

a
3x−2
b
3x+4
c
2x−1
d
2x
e
3x+1
Submit

decision.explanation: At (1,1), f=0, f_y=-x cos(x-y)=-1, and f_xx=2 cos(x-y)-x sin(x-y)=2. Each displacement vector has first entry x-1. The six missing expressions therefore sum to 0-1+(x-1)+(x-1)+2+(x-1)=3x-2.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y),
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}∗ & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.
after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y) & x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y) & -x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈0+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
0+(-1)+(x-1)+(x-1)+2+(x-1)=3x-2.
$$

For the function f:R2→R, defined as

f(x,y)=xsin⁡(x−y),

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[11] is given by

f(x)≈∗+[1∗][∗y−1]+12[∗y−1]T[∗−1−10][∗y−1].

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.

a
3x−2
b
3x+4
c
2x−1
d
2x
e
3x+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defened by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have the following:

f′(x)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y],f″(x)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

  • Calculating the value of the function, we have f(1,1)=0.

  • Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following: f′(x)=[sin⁡(x−y)+xcos⁡(x−y)−xcos⁡(x−y)]f′(1,1)=[1−1]

  • Calculating the second derivative, we have the following: f″(x)=[2cos⁡(x−y)−xsin⁡(x−y)xsin⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x−y)xsin⁡(x−y)−cos⁡(x−y)−xsin⁡(x−y)]f″(1,1)=[2−1−10]

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

f(x)≈0+[1−1][x−1y−1]+12[x−1y−1]T[2−1−10][x−1y−1]

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

0+(−1)+(x−1)+(x−1)+2+(x−1)=3x−2.

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}∗ & -e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ ∗\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ ∗\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}].

after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3x-y} & -{e}^{3x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,2) & =[\begin{aligned}3e & -e\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x-y} & -3{e}^{3x-y} \\ -3{e}^{3x-y} & {e}^{3x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,2) & =[\begin{aligned}9e & -3e \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈e+[\begin{aligned}3e & -e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}9e & -3e \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
e+3e+(y-2)+(y-2)+9e+(-3e)=2y+10e-4.
$$

{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}

$$

$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$

$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+y}+2x & \frac{1}{x+y}+3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+2 & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+6y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+4+(y-1)+(y-1)+5+(y-1)=3y+7.
$$

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+y}+2x & \frac{1}{x+y}+3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+2 & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}} & -\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}+6y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+4+(y-1)+(y-1)+5+(y-1)=3y+7.
$$

content.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$

$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}].

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2y} & 2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2y} & 2{e}^{x+2y} \\ 2{e}^{x+2y} & 4{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+2+x+x+2+x=3x+5.
$$

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈2+[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2) & ≈2+[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2+[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2+(-2)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,-1) & =-e, & \,{f}^{′}(1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,-1) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,0).$
after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-e, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & ≈-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 0+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-e+[\begin{aligned}-e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-e & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-e+2e+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}e \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =e+\frac{1}{2}(-e+1) \\  & =\frac{e+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$

$$
